signals.title: Achieving near-zero-downtime scaling in Elastic Expert Parallelism | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Achieving near-zero-downtime scaling in Elastic Expert Parallelism

October 19, 2026 12 min read

Itay Alroy (NVIDIA)

Table of Contents

Traditionally, changing the number of GPUs in a vLLM service required adding or removing entire model replicas or restarting the engine with a different GPU count. As models grow larger, each replica needs more GPUs, so scaling by replica adds or removes GPUs in increasingly large increments. Restarting vLLM to scale DeepSeek V4 Pro from 16 to 20 GB200 GPUs stopped serving for 197 seconds (see the performance section for details), leaving those expensive GPUs allocated without generating tokens.

In our first Elastic EP post, we showed how vLLM could add or remove GPUs from a running DEP deployment (data-parallel attention with expert-parallel MoE) without restarting it. While we avoided a restart, serving still stopped throughout reconfiguration as we initialized new workers, prepared the expanded communication groups, loaded model weights, and repeated kernel warmup and CUDA graph capture. In our DeepSeek V4 Pro benchmark, this pause lasted 100 seconds when scaling from 16 to 20 GPUs and 56 seconds when scaling back to 16 GPUs (full details in the performance section).

In this post, we describe how asynchronous preparation and NIXL EP enabled Elastic EP reconfiguration with near-zero downtime. In the same benchmark, we reduced downtime to 0.82 seconds when scaling from 16 to 20 GPUs and 1.96 seconds when scaling back to 16 GPUs, allowing us to scale up and down with almost no impact on serving performance.

...

## Performance on DeepSeek V4 Pro

All experiments in this section used DeepSeek V4 Pro on GB200 GPUs, with TP=1 and DP/EP sizes of 16 and 20. Model weights were pre-downloaded in safetensors format on shared Lustre storage and loaded using the default `--load-format auto`. Measurements used warm kernel-compilation caches (Triton, TileLang, and FlashInfer).

### Scale-up and scale-down timings

The table shows which stages run while serving is paused and which run in the background while existing workers continue serving.

| Stage | A: Blocking | B: Async preparation | C: Async preparation + graph reuse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initialize joining workers | Serving paused | Background | Background |
| Prepare target communication | Serving paused | Background | Background |
| Transfer model weights | Serving paused | Background | Background |
| Warmup and graph capture on joining workers | Serving paused | Serving paused | Background |
| Warmup and graph capture on existing workers | Serving paused | Serving paused | Not needed (existing graphs stay valid) |
| Activate the target topology | Serving paused | Serving paused | Serving paused |

Configuration C is supported only by NIXL EP.

- Downtime: the observed serving interruption, when in-flight requests stop progressing and new requests are not admitted.
- Total time: the duration of the full scaling operation, including preparation.

The two durations are measured separately.

| Metric | A: Blocking | B: Async preparation | C: Async preparation + graph reuse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16 to 20 GPUs: downtime | 99.62 s | 58.04 s | 0.82 s |
| 20 to 16 GPUs: downtime | 56.25 s | 44.07 s | 1.96 s |
| 16 to 20 GPUs: total time | 99.72 s | 97.27 s | 92.34 s |
| 20 to 16 GPUs: total time | 56.21 s | 51.46 s | 9.32 s |

All configurations passed numerical correctness checks, including checks on every joining worker.

...

## Try Elastic EP

Background preparation, CUDA graph reuse, and independent graph capture on joining workers are all available today in the latest vLLM and NIXL releases. Install them with pip and start using Elastic EP.

For a complete usage example, see the `cuda_graphs_heavy_nixl_ep` case in vLLM's Elastic EP test. The example includes the server configuration and scaling API calls. It scales from two GPUs to four and back while sending requests, checking serving during preparation and model accuracy around each resize.

signals.title: ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars
signals.excerpt:
# ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars

OpenViking from ByteDance's Volcengine treats agent memory, knowledge and skills as a virtual filesystem, crossing 40,000 GitHub stars.

 By Marcello Babbili · AI-assisted newsroom October 19, 2026 3 min read 

Image generated by OpenAI

ByteDance's Volcengine team published OpenViking, an open-source context database that treats everything an AI agent knows as files under a `viking://` filesystem, and the project crossed 40,000 stars on GitHub this week after gaining 105 stars in a single day on the platform's trending list S¹.

The approach challenges how most agent builders work today: stitching together separate systems for retrieval-augmented generation (the standard method for feeding documents into a model), conversation memory, and tool or skill management. OpenViking collapses all three into one virtual filesystem that an agent can browse and read on demand P² P⁴.

...

My read: This is the first agent-memory project I've seen that refuses to separate knowledge from memory from skills at the storage layer. Most teams I watch are still gluing a vector database to a chat-history buffer and calling it done. The filesystem metaphor is elegant, but the benchmark numbers are entirely self-reported and nobody outside the Volcengine team has verified them. I'd want to see independent tau2-bench results before believing the performance claims, and the 40,000-star count tells me about GitHub momentum, not production readiness.

...

### One filesystem, three context types

The Viking team, part of ByteDance's cloud infrastructure arm Volcengine, organises context into three types: resources for reference material, memories for information retained from interactions, and skills for task procedures P⁴. Each piece of context loads in three tiers: L0, a one-sentence abstract; L1, a core overview; and L2, the full original data S¹. An agent scans the L0 summaries to decide what it needs, then drills down to L2 only for relevant items, which keeps token consumption down.

When a conversation session ends, OpenViking commits and archives it as Markdown files that a developer can read and edit by hand S¹. Memories sit in readable text, not a binary store, which makes debugging and correction straightforward.

...

### The benchmarks nobody has checked

The project reports evaluation results on two benchmarks: LoCoMo, which tests long-conversation user memory, and tau2-bench, which tests multi-turn agent tasks S¹. Version 0.3.22 used Doubao 2.0 Pro, Volcengine's own vision-language model, for the memory evaluation S¹. These results are self-reported. The repository does not include peer-reviewed or third-party-audited benchmark data, and the README is the maintainers' description of their own work, not an independent review.

A developer who wants to try the system without committing to an install can use OpenViking Studio, a browser-based demo that requires no setup S¹.

The repository is written primarily in Python and carries the volcengine organisation label on GitHub, though the about page confirms the team sits inside ByteDance's Volcengine unit P².

Until an independent team reproduces the LoCoMo or tau2-bench results, the 40,000-star count measures interest, not proof.

signals.title: llama.cpp adds Q1_0, Q2_0 quant support for Hexagon NPUs
signals.excerpt:
llama.cpp adds Q1_0, Q2_0 quant support for Hexagon NPUs

Quantization Inference and serving· 17 Oct 2026

# llama.cpp adds Q1_0, Q2_0 quant support for Hexagon NPUs

Snapdragon devices get another notch of compression for on-device inference

## The facts

- Release b11716 of llama.cpp adds support for Q1_0 and Q2_0 quantisation formats on Qualcomm Hexagon NPUs (pull request #30122)
- Changes include enabling Q1_0 weights in the 2D HMX MUL_MAT path and adding Q2_0 support with cleanup of stale asserts and special cases
- Work includes fixes to the MUL_MAT_NX tiling assumption, since Q1/Q2 formats use non-square tiles rather than the square tiling assumed elsewhere
- Multiple commits optimise Q1_0 and Q2_0 vec_dots and layout to reduce unpack and vrmpy overhead
- Co-authored by Max Krasnyansky of Qualcomm; builds are available for Linux arm64 and Android arm64 targeting Snapdragon CPU, Adreno GPU and Hexagon NPU

The latest llama.cpp pre-release, tagged b11716, adds support for two low-bit quantisation formats on Qualcomm's Hexagon neural processing unit. Q1_0 and Q2_0 compress model weights to roughly one or two bits each. The change, merged via pull request #30122, lets the Hexagon backend run these compressed models through the existing 2D HMX matrix-multiply path used for tiled tensor formats.

Getting there required more than flipping a flag. Q1_0 and Q2_0 weights use non-square tiles, which broke an assumption baked into llama.cpp's MUL_MAT_NX routine: that tiling would always be square. The patch generalises that path instead of special-casing it. Several follow-up commits strip out stale asserts and special cases left over from earlier work. They also tighten the vec_dot routines and memory layout for both formats, cutting the overhead from unpacking and vector multiply-accumulate (vrmpy) operations.

The work was co-authored by Max Krasnyansky of Qualcomm. That underscores the chipmaker's continued hand in llama.cpp's Hexagon backend. Build artefacts for this release include a dedicated Linux arm64 target and an Android arm64 target. Both cover Snapdragon CPU, Adreno GPU and Hexagon NPU execution. The usual Linux, Windows, macOS and openEuler builds remain too, across CUDA, Vulkan, ROCm, SYCL and OpenVINO backends.

...

## Why it matters

Sub-2-bit quantisation on Hexagon NPUs means developers can push larger models onto Snapdragon phones and laptops without falling back to the CPU or GPU path. Anyone targeting on-device inference on Snapdragon hardware should re-test memory and latency against this build before locking in a quant format.

signals.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Expands Beyond Text to Support Code, Images, Video, and Audio - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
Oct 19, 2026 2 min read 

by

- Sergio De Simone 

Based on Gemma 4 and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-weight, multimodal embedding model designed to make semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more efficient while optimizing performance for on-device deployment.

> Designed to run on consumer hardware such as mobile devices and laptops, EmbeddingGemma 2 delivers low-latency semantic representations for on-device applications, like search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), classification, and clustering.

Thanks to its multimodal capabilities, EmbeddingGemma 2 supports a wide range of retrieval tasks, including finding relevant documents, screenshots, and recordings in response to a query, searching source code using natural language, and retrieving video content based on textual descriptions.

EmbeddingGemma 2's key feature, Google says, is its ability to represent text, code, images, video, and audio in a unified 768-dimensional embedding space. This enables developers to build retrieval systems that search across different media types without maintaining separate, incompatible embedding spaces for different media types.

> Despite coming from different modalities, the embeddings generated by EmbeddingGemma 2 occupy the same dimensional space and can be compared on their semantic similarity.

The model allows developers to load only the encoders required for their applications, scaling from 270 million parameters for text and code to 740 million for full multimodal support. According to Google, the model "significantly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1 on code search and technical retrieval, making it ideal for local codebase indexing and agentic code search".

...

EmbeddingGemma 2 supports Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), which allows embeddings to be truncated into shorter, unit-length vectors, reducing storage requirements. For example, storing a million 768-dimensional vectors at bfloat16 precision takes roughly 1.5 GB of memory, while truncating them to 128 dimensions requires just 250 MB, bringing a sixfold reduction. However, this implies a retrieval quality trade-off. Google therefore recommends using truncation only when storage or search speed require it. At 128 dimensions, the model retains approximately 90% of quality with text, but performance drops to around 75% for image, video, and speech retrieval.

...

EmbeddingGemma was introduced last year with a focus on "offline and privacy-sensitive scenarios, such as searching across personal files locally, running mobile RAG pipelines with Gemma 3n, or building domain-specific chatbots". EmbeddingGemma 2 is available on Hugging Face.

signals.excerpt:

AI benchmark news October 17, 2026

# Vera Rubin NVL72 benchmark: AA-AgentPerf results on October 15, 2026

Artificial Analysis, October 15, 2026: Vera Rubin NVL72 serves up to ~5.7x GB300 NVL72's throughput per MW.

By Elena Marsh 5 min read

Artificial Analysis published the first AA-AgentPerf results for NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 on October 15, 2026. In its Vera Rubin NVL72 benchmark, the rack serves up to about 5.7 times the total throughput per megawatt of the GB300 NVL72 it replaces on DeepSeek V4 Pro, about 5.4 times on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, about 3.0 times on GLM-5.2 and about 2.8 times on Kimi K3. Each is the largest gap at one per-user speed; at peak throughput the lead is 1.14 to 1.45 times.

Vera Rubin NVL72 is NVIDIA’s rack-scale system of the Rubin generation, with 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs in one NVLink domain. What NVIDIA has announced about the platform is collected in our Nvidia Rubin explainer, and the chip sits alongside its predecessors in our AI chips table.

...

## What AA-AgentPerf measures

AA-AgentPerf is a hardware benchmark built around coding agents rather than chat. According to Artificial Analysis’s methodology, it replays real coding-agent trajectories, produced by agents resolving issues in public code repositories, at a range of concurrency levels. Each simulated agent works through three trajectories in sequence and pauses after each reply for a tool-call time taken from real tool-call durations.

That traffic looks different from fixed-length prompts. Requests carry up to 132K input tokens, replies are often a short tool call, and on average 97% of a request’s input tokens repeat the previous request. Artificial Analysis says this makes KV cache capacity and reuse, uneven prefill and time to first token decisive. Our KV cache explainer covers why a repeated prefix can be served from cache instead of being processed again.

The headline metric is total throughput (input and output tokens, about 96% of them cached input) per megawatt of measured GPU power, plotted against per-user output speed at the 25th percentile. Measured power covers each GPU and its HBM as reported by NVIDIA’s telemetry, and excludes CPUs, networking and cooling.

...

## The results

| Model | Largest lead per MW vs GB300 NVL72 | At per-user speed | Lead at peak throughput (tokens/s per MW) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek V4 Pro | ~5.7x | ~190 tok/s | 1.14x (272M vs 239M) |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | ~5.4x | ~580 tok/s | 1.45x (571M vs 395M) |
| GLM-5.2 | ~3.0x | ~165 tok/s | 1.35x (272M vs 201M) |
| Kimi K3 | ~2.8x | ~67 tok/s | 1.26x (70M vs 56M) |

Source: Artificial Analysis, results as of October 15, 2026.

# Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model

October 19, 2026

## Abstract

We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

signals.title: NVIDIA Vera CPUs double throughput for Modal Sandboxes
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA Vera CPUs double throughput for Modal Sandboxes

Source: Modal• October 19, 2026 at 02:09 PM

# NVIDIA Vera CPUs double throughput for Modal Sandboxes

We benchmarked NVIDIA's new Arm-based Vera CPU on agentic Sandbox workloads. Under heavy load, it completes far more tasks than the x86 and Graviton alternatives, without sacrificing latency.

Last week, NVIDIA hand-delivered Modal’s first Vera CPU server to our SF office. It’s now purring away in a server rack, and we’re pretty excited about what it could mean for Modal Sandboxes and, consequently, Modal users.

Vera is NVIDIA’s new Arm-compatible CPU, built for the Vera Rubin GPU platform but also available as a standalone CPU server.

Supporting Arm would be a huge change for Modal, coming from a long history exclusively running x86 machines. We’d need to make changes across our infrastructure and image build system to support an entirely different CPU architecture, but the benchmarks are impressive: a 2x increase on throughput. With this, the NVIDIA Vera CPU becomes an incredibly compelling option for powering Modal Sandboxes.

...

## Benchmarking the Vera CPU

To test Vera, we built a set of representative workloads and benchmarks for agentic Sandboxes.

Creating an “agentic” benchmark is a challenging task, given most of the work done on the servers is not CPU bound, and there’s no specific dimension we’d want to optimize for. Where a DB workload could optimize for disk I/O and an image processing workload could optimize SIMD, for sandboxes we needed to come up with a simulator that is both concurrent and heterogeneous: a big ol’ bag of chaos we could throw at the CPU.

From this we developed Agentless Agent Bench, a collection of 50 Terminal-Bench oracle solutions and verifiers, stripped of all network calls and prewarmed in concurrent Docker containers, isolating just the tasks actually performed on the CPU by agents and RL - compilation, file grepping, git operations, device emulation, and more.

Running the benchmark shows us both linear task completion time, and concurrent throughput metrics.

Below are results showing per-task latency for a selection of Terminal-Bench tasks you’d reasonably see an agent running in your sandboxes. This experiment was run on a machine without load, serially, so the results show pure straightline latency.

Seeing these results first, I was admittedly skeptical. Across the 50 tasks we benchmarked, Vera often performed better than the other CPUs, but not always, and not by a particularly large margin.

...

During one of our onsites at NVIDIA HQ, I vividly remember first seeing these results, and being unable to believe how they could be true.

Our early benchmarking runs show up to double the task throughput on Vera compared with an equivalent x86 GNR machine, despite individual task latency measuring equal to, or sometimes even lower than, the x86 machine. This is because Vera does not slow down as jobs accumulate but rips through each one at the original pace.

When asked, the Vera team confirmed that these results are not surprising. It was at this moment I became a Vera believer.

signals.title: Models That Use Tools | Archipelag.io
signals.excerpt:
October 19, 2026 

# Models That Use Tools

Archipelag.io now ships with a chat harness: models on the network can call tools, in the web chat, through the OpenAI-compatible API, from the SDKs and the CLI, and on phone Islands too.

 Raffael Schneider · 5 min read

Ask a small language model what 17.5% of 2,340 is and it will answer with total confidence and, often enough, the wrong number. Ask it what day it is and it will guess. Neither is a flaw you can train away in a model that fits on a laptop. What you can do is let it ask for help.

That’s what shipped this week. Every chat on Archipelag.io can now use tools: the model decides it needs a calculator, a clock or a lookup, says so in a structured way, gets the result back, and only then answers. It works in the web chat, through the API, from the SDKs and the CLI, and on desktop, server and phone Islands alike.

...

In the web chat, there’s a new Tools toggle (it routes your chat to a desktop or server Island). Turn it on and ask something a model shouldn’t do in its head:

> What’s 17.5% of 2,340, and what day of the week is it?

The model calls `calculate` with `2340 * 0.175`, calls `current_time`, gets `409.5` and today’s date back, and writes its answer from facts instead of guesses. You see each step as it happens: the call, the result, then the reply.

The built-in tools are deliberately plain:

- calculate: arithmetic, through a small expression parser (no `eval`, ever).
- current_time: the date and time, in UTC or at any UTC offset.
- search_cargos: looks up which models the network offers, so you can ask the chat which model is best for your task.
- generate_image: when an image Cargo is available, the chat model can hand off a picture request to it, and the image appears in the conversation.

Reasoning models also show their work now. When a model thinks before answering, that thinking is kept apart from the answer and folded away under a “Thought for N words” line you can open, and replies render as proper Markdown.

...

## Your own tools, through the API

The built-ins are for the web chat. The real point is the API, which speaks the same `tools` and `tool_calls` format as OpenAI’s Chat Completions, streaming included. If your code already talks to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, you change the base URL and your existing tool definitions just work.

The Python and JavaScript SDKs (0.2.0) wrap the whole loop. Write a function, mark it as a tool, and the SDK handles the back-and-forth until the model has its answer:

```python
from archipelag import Client, tool

@tool
def stock_level(sku: str) -> int:
    """How many units of a product are in the warehouse."""
    return warehouse.count(sku)

client = Client(api_key=...)
result = client.run_agent(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "Do we have enough SKU-1142 for an order of 40?"}],
    tools=[stock_level],
)
print(result.content)

```

Your function runs on your machine. The Island that runs the model only ever sees the tool’s name, its description, and the result you choose to send back. It never gets your database, your files or your credentials, which matters on a network where the computer doing the thinking belongs to someone else.

The JavaScript SDK has the same thing as `runAgent`, and the `island` CLI now has an interactive `island chat` for trying models from a terminal.

...

Desktop and server Islands (v0.6.0) render each conversation with the model’s own chat template, the one it was trained on, so tool definitions reach it in exactly the format it expects. When tools are offered, generation is constrained by a grammar that only switches on once the model starts a tool call. Before that, it writes freely. Once it commits to a call, it can only produce well-formed JSON. The call comes back as structured `tool_calls`, not as text you’d have to parse and hope about.

...

signals.title: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
signals.excerpt:
## Story

# TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
Published October 19, 2026
Régis Pierrard
TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.
## TorchNeuron
TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, `torch.compile` and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.
Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with `pip install torch-neuronx`.
## New backend, native interface in HF libraries
To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.
TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes `neuron` as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and `torch.compile`.
For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.
#### Inference
Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the `device\_map=neuron` argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.
The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.
```py

...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig))
    script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config()
    main(script_args, training_args, model_args)
```
Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a `DistributedConfig` with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in `model\_init\_kwargs`, `SFTTrainer` passes it to `from\_pretrained`, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an `--fsdp` flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.
Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:
* **Static shapes.** The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in `torch.compile` and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes.
* **`torch.compile` on.** Passing `--torch\_compile true` is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, `torch.compile` detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure.
* **Async weight loading off.** The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with `HF\_DEACTIVATE\_ASYNC\_LOAD=1`.
The command below launches training with `torchrun`, which starts one process per NeuronCore. `TP\_SIZE` and `FSDP\_SIZE` set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching `--nproc\_per\_node`. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.
```sh
TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \
    --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
    --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \
    --dataset_train_split train_sft \
    --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --max_length 2048 \
    --packing true \
    --packing_strategy wrapped \
    --learning_rate 2e-5 \
    --warmup_steps 0.03 \
    --num_train_epochs 1 \
    --logging_steps 2 \
    --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
    --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \
    --save_only_model true \
    --torch_compile true
```
We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a `trn2.48xlarge` instance.
Training runs to completion, and `trainer.save\_model` writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Chinese artificial intelligence company MiniMax has released M3.1 Flash, a new AI model designed to handle complex enterprise workflows, software development and computer-use tasks at dramatically lower costs than many competing frontier models — including the popular Chinese rival DeepSeek during peak hours. 

MiniMax says its new model operates nearly 3X faster than its predecessor while reducing overall usage costs for AI agents by 70%. We’ll dig more into how teams are cutting context and token costs at VentureBeat’s Agentic Infrastructure Stack Summit in San Francisco on October 28.

But the more interesting evidence comes from independent testing: Artificial Analysis has awarded M3.1 Flash a score of 42 on its Intelligence Index, up 13 points from the previous MiniMax M3, with a per-task evaluation cost less than half that of its predecessor.

That puts M3.1 Flash on par with Z.ai's GLM-5.3 Flash, just ahead of Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash, and within striking distance of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 — another new, inexpensive Chinese AI model — which scores 45.

There is, however, an important limitation: Artificial Analysis also found that while M3.1 Flash answered more than half of its factual knowledge questions correctly, it demonstrated an exceptionally high tendency to generate incorrect answers rather than acknowledge uncertainty.

The results underscore both the growing competitiveness of inexpensive Chinese AI models and the trade-offs enterprises must consider when deploying them for tasks requiring accuracy, reliability and minimal human supervision.

In its official announcement, MiniMax emphasizes the model's ability to execute extended sequences of actions across business software, coding environments and computer interfaces.

However, Artificial Analysis found that MiniMax attempted nearly every question, producing a 93% hallucination rate under the benchmark's definition.

signals.title: Neo4j joins the context cavalcade with suite for informing AI agents | TechTarget
signals.excerpt:
Neo4j joins the context cavalcade with suite for informing AI agents | TechTarget
## Context Engine is a set of features that enables the vendor's customers to build knowledge layers for agents to access to inform their actions.
By
* Eric Avidon, Senior News Writer
Published: 20 Oct 2026
Add Neo4j to the list of data management providers offering capabilities designed to connect AI agents with the context they require to deliver accurate responses.
The graph database specialist on Tuesday launched Context Engine, a collection of tools that customers can use to create a knowledge layer for agents to call on when responding to user queries and carrying out prescribed tasks and processes.
The suite includes Business Ontology, which is a model that enables enterprises to map contextually relevant information in Neo4j, Context Build and Runtime so customers can build ontologies from data sources such as Databricks and Snowflake, Context Studio where users can manage and govern their ontologies, and Context Memory to provide agents with persistent memory.
"[Context Engine] is as significant as the broader enterprise shift toward Agentic AI, representing an essential evolution for Neo4j and its customers," William McKnight, president of McKnight Consulting, told TechTarget.
Neo4j is particularly well-positioned to help customers build knowledge layers for agents given its specialization in graph technology, he added, noting that graph modeling -- unlike vector search and relational database joins -- not only connects related entities but also the semantics related to why and how they relate.
"This delivers superior contextual grounding by allowing agents to execute targeted, deterministic traversals that provide precise, high-signal facts directly to the model while eliminating … context bloat, token bleed and topological blind spots," McKnight said.
## Aiding understanding
Agents are the new data consumers. But agents don't have the same institutional knowledge or hardcoded logic as the humans and business applications that have historically been the main consumers of data. They require a map to discover relevant context spread across databases, applications, documents and other sources of business logic.
Without that map, agents will deliver confident but incorrect outputs that could have significant negative consequences.
> What was missing was an explicit link between data types, which would have made it easier for AI to make the correct connections. Neo4j Context Engine packages the work we've done with customers so far into a shared knowledge layer that every agent can draw on more reliably.
>
**> Sudhir Hasbe
**> President of technology and chief product officer, Neo4j
Consequently, connecting agents with relevant business logic has been a dominant trend throughout 2026 with hyperscalers such as AWS and Microsoft, platform providers including Databricks and Snowflake, and niche specialists from Alteryx to ThoughtSpot all adding capabilities aiming to improve the data discovery and retrieval process.
Neo4j's Context Engine, like the data discovery and retrieval capabilities added by other data management providers, is designed to enable AI tools to operationalize the contextually relevant information they need to understand what to do. Meanwhile, the specific impetus for developing the suite came from observing hundreds of customers struggle to build agents that accurately interpreted terms such as "account" and supplier" when such terms were used differently across enterprise systems, according to Sudhir Hasbe, Neo4j's president of technology and chief product officer.
"What was missing was an explicit link between data types, which would have made it easier for AI to make the correct connections," he said. "Neo4j Context Engine packages the work we've done with customers so far into a shared knowledge layer that every agent can draw on more reliably."
With the initial version of Context Engine generally available, the feature-set is now part of Neo4j's ongoing attempt to help customers build knowledge layers for AI, Hasbe continued.
"Expanding the knowledge layer to make AI more effective and efficient remains a major focus, and Context Engine is a big part of that," he said. "We're also continuing to grow our AI customer base and our ecosystem of partners to ensure customers see the best ROI from AI."
While Neo4j's Context Engine is not the first such suite of capabilities to hit the market, it is distinguished from competing offerings by running queries within its database rather than forcing customers to stitch together complex context retrieval pipelines, according to McKnight.
"Neo4j's advantage is running index-free adjacency and Cypher queries directly within its core transactional database rather than orchestrating across disparate external services," McKnight said.
## The right stuff
As with any new offering, Neo4j's Context Engine is only valuable if it truly enables the vendor's customers to build an effective knowledge layer that AI agents can use as a source for decisions and actions. While the current iteration brings together domain ontology, agent memory and query execution, McKnight notes that as it is currently built, Context Engine functions solely as a read-only knowledge layer.
It lacks capabilities such as native change data capture connectors and bidirectional write-back capabilities so agents can safely send changes back to enterprise systems of record.
"To transition from a static context cache into an active operational substrate, Context Engine must move beyond read-only retrieval," McKnight said.
In addition, he suggested that Neo4j could better serve existing customers and perhaps attract new ones by expanding zero-copy federated querying capabilities across lakehouse architectures such as Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake and improve its centralized governance capabilities to reduce "graph sprawl" across an organization's business units.
"Most importantly, to convert traditional relational and data warehouse teams at scale, Neo4j should publish independent, third-party benchmarks proving query throughput, retrieval latency and multi-year total cost of ownerships advantages for high-concurrency enterprise workloads," McKnight said.
*Eric Avidon is a senior news writer for Informa TechTarget and a journalist with more than three decades of experience. He covers analytics and data management.*

signals.title: Arm Community
signals.excerpt:
ExecuTorch was designed to eliminate this gap. Arm MCU support has been available through the Ethos-U NPU, and the Cortex-M backend extends it to Cortex-M CPUs, so a model can run on parts with or without an accelerator. The trained PyTorch model is exported, quantized and lowered for the device within the same stack that serves models on mobile, desktop and server.

...

## The Cortex-M backend

Figure 1: ExecuTorch model compilation and deployment workflow for Arm Cortex-M CPUs.

The ExecuTorch Cortex-M backend replaces standard PyTorch operators with CMSIS-NN-backed custom operators through ahead-of-time compiler passes. At inference time, these operators call directly into Arm's CMSIS-NN library, an open-source collection of optimized neural network kernels for Cortex-M processors.

Key properties:

- CMSIS-NN accelerated. Quantized operations (linear, conv, add, mul, softmax, activations, etc.) are replaced with optimized implementations that call CMSIS-NN functions and additional optimized Cortex-M implementations directly.
- Target-aware compilation. The CPU variant (M0 through M85) and ISA tier are specified at compile time, so the correct CMSIS-NN backend is selected, eliminating runtime dispatch overhead.
- Purpose-built quantizer. Produces INT8 quantized graphs matching the data layout requirements of CMSIS-NN kernels, using PyTorch's PT2E quantization framework.
- Single compiler toolchain. The Cortex-M lowering path operates directly on the ExecuTorch edge dialect, keeping the compilation pipeline simple and debuggable.

...

Many Cortex-M MCUs pair the CPU with an Arm Ethos-U NPU such as the U55, U65, or U85. ExecuTorch's EthosUPartitioner delegates supported operations to the NPU via the Vela compiler, and operations left outside the partition run on the Cortex-M CPU within the same graph.

The Cortex-M passes run after Ethos-U partitioning and reuse the quantization parameters already in the graph. This allows a model quantized with EthosUQuantizer to use CMSIS-NN for CPU operations whose quantization, layout and shape constraints meet the Cortex-M backend requirements. Otherwise they fall back to ExecuTorch's portable kernels, which are functional but not accelerated.

...

In our measurements, ExecuTorch achieves 2.3% to 10.6% lower inference latency on three of the four models. Autoencoder latency is nearly identical, with ExecuTorch taking 0.27% longer. Memory is where the two frameworks diverge more sharply. The measured model/operator/core footprint is up to 21.1% less flash across all four models, and less RAM on three of the four, including 46.1% less on the Autoencoder. ResNet-8 is the exception, using 1.2% more RAM than TFLM.

The released configuration defaults to two recurrent loops and sets the maximum position count to 262144. It combines sliding attention with full attention. These settings describe the model configuration rather than a guarantee that any particular machine can serve the maximum context at useful speed. Model configuration.

The practical question is how much work the model should do before producing its next token. Reusing parameters lets developers explore that question without swapping the checkpoint. It does not remove the need to measure latency, memory use and answer quality together. A smaller output is not automatically a faster answer when each generated token takes more computation. vLLM review.

NVIDIA recommends starting with two loops. Its reported results show that increasing the loop count does not improve every benchmark. Those measurements belong to NVIDIA, and the BF16 results should not be assumed to describe a quantized download. Model card.

...

## Available weights are ahead of stable runtime support

The vLLM integration is an open pull request. Its implementation work began before the weight release and remains separate from a stable package release. Developers should check that the version they choose actually contains Dory support rather than assume that a generic installation command is sufficient. vLLM review.

This distinction matters for deployment planning. A public checkpoint gives developers access to the model, while a runtime integration determines whether their serving stack can load it correctly. Teams maintaining production services should treat a review branch as an evaluation dependency and keep the exact revision with their results. vLLM review.

The llama.cpp integration is still marked draft. Its author reports support for one through four loops and tests with BF16 and two quantized formats. The same report lists incomplete long context qualification and full continuous integration, with Metal untested. These are contributor observations rather than independent ByteForward tests. llama.cpp review.

# APUS AI开源Reflex Agent：速度快3倍、主打无限上下文

APUS AI 宣布开源旗下 Agent 产品 Reflex Agent。根据公开信息，该产品主打两项特性：响应速度比 Claude Code 快约 3 倍，以及实现“真正的无限上下文”。

对 AI 编程类 Agent 来说，响应延迟和上下文长度是两项直接影响可用性的指标。延迟决定开发者调用 Agent 时的等待成本，上下文长度则决定 Agent 能否在一次任务中持续掌握跨文件、跨模块的信息。目前主流的编程 Agent 大多在有限 AI 词典：上下文窗口">上下文窗口内运行，处理长任务时通常要依赖摘要、检索或分段处理，因此容易造成信息丢失和重复读取。如果“无限上下文”能够在工程上稳定实现，那么在大仓库、长周期任务中的连续性有望明显改善。

选择开源，也意味着这些能力将交给外部开发者复现和检验。需要指出的是，上述性能与上下文能力均来自厂商的公开表述，实际表现仍需在真实项目中验证，包括在不同规模代码库、不同任务类型下的延迟与稳定性。

目前，热点信息中尚未披露该项目的具体实现方式、开源许可证与部署要求。对关注 Agent 基础设施的开发者而言，值得跟进官方仓库与后续技术文档，观察“无限上下文”究竟指模型侧能力、工程侧的记忆管理，还是两者的组合。

signals.title: Crusoe Keeps 4-Bit Weights to Cut LoRA Memory by 75% | StartupHub.ai
signals.excerpt:
# Crusoe Keeps 4-Bit Weights to Cut LoRA Memory by 75%

Crusoe shows how storing frozen base weights in 4-bit and dequantizing in-kernel cuts LoRA memory by up to 75% without accuracy loss.

StartupHub.ai Staff Oct 17 at 1:17 PM 2 min read

Crusoe keeps base weights in 4-bit and dequantizes inside the kernel· Crusoe Blog

Crusoe Blog says its post-training team built LoRA training that keeps frozen base weights in 4-bit and dequantizes them inside the kernel.

LoRA, or Low-Rank Adaptation, freezes the base model and trains two small matrices that add about one percent of parameters.

A 1 trillion parameter model like Kimi-K2.6 needs at least 2 terabytes for base weights in bf16, or four HGX H100 nodes, according to Crusoe.

In unmerged LoRA inference Crusoe keeps the base path in mxfp4 with activations quantized to mxfp8 while the adapter path stays in bf16.

On Blackwell the matmul runs natively in mxfp4, but on Hopper Crusoe still stores 4-bit and dequantizes to bf16 inside the kernel.

In the backward pass Crusoe needs only gradients for A, B and the input, so frozen W never needs a bf16 copy or optimizer update.

DeepSeek V4 also cuts single-token FLOPs and KV cache to about ten percent of DeepSeek V3.2 at one million tokens, per Codersera's setup guide.

Crusoe reports no accuracy drop from the train-inference precision mismatch, but the result relies on the quantization passthrough assumption used in quantization-aware training.

Serverless Fine-Tuning with this dequant-on-the-fly kernel is now generally available in Crusoe Intelligence Foundry and bills per training token.
